\section*{The Model}

\subsection*{Environment}

Time is continuous. Demand $X_t$ governs the revenue available to frontier AI labs; its units are fixed by the capacity normalization of \texttt{sec-calibration}, so levels below are relative. Demand follows a geometric Brownian motion with regime-dependent drift and common volatility:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-gbm}]}
dX_t = \mu_s X_t \, dt + \sigma X_t \, dW_t, \quad s \in \{L, H\},
\end{equation*}

where $W_t$ is a standard Brownian motion, $s$ indexes the demand regime, and $\sigma > 0$ is the common volatility parameter.



\subsection*{Technology}

\subsubsection*{Training-inference allocation}

- \textbf{Low regime} ($L$, pre-AGI): revenue derives from \emph{inference}, that is, from serving current demand. Firm $i$'s flow revenue is:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-revenue-L}]}
\pi_i^L(X) = X \cdot [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha,
\end{equation*}

where $\alpha$ is the revenue elasticity of capacity.



- \textbf{High regime} ($H$, post-AGI): revenue derives from \emph{training compute}, which I read as a proxy for model capability. Firm $i$'s flow revenue is:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-revenue-H}]}
\pi_i^H(X) = X \cdot (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha,
\end{equation*}

with the same elasticity applied to training compute.



\subsection*{Single-Firm Benchmark}

Two further properties hold without being assumed. The effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K)$ defined below is twice continuously differentiable in $\phi \in (0,1)$ for every $K > 0$, as a property of its functional form. And at the baseline the \emph{L-regime insufficiency condition}

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-l-insufficiency}]}
\frac{1 - 1/\beta_L^+}{\alpha} \geq 1
\end{equation*}

holds (the ratio is $1.67$, with $\beta_L^+ \approx 3.01$ the positive root of the L-regime characteristic equation given below). It is a description, not an assumption: it says that the standalone L-regime scale problem has no interior optimum, so L-regime revenue alone does not pin down an investment. It plays no role in the solution that follows and licenses no simplification of the option value. At the baseline values of the other parameters it holds wherever (A2) does, since (A2) requires $\alpha < 0.534$ and \texttt{eq-l-insufficiency} requires $\alpha \leq 0.67$.



\subsubsection*{Installed value}

In the absorbing high regime, the value of installed capacity depends on training compute:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-installed-value-H}]}
V_H(X, K, \phi) = \frac{X (\phi K)^\alpha}{r - \mu_H} - \frac{\delta K}{r} = A_H \cdot X \cdot (\phi K)^\alpha - \frac{\delta K}{r},
\end{equation*}



where $A_H = 1/(r - \mu_H)$. In the low regime, installed value combines current inference revenue and the expected continuation value from a switch to $H$:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-installed-value-L}]}
V_L(X, K, \phi) = A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K) \cdot X - \frac{\delta K}{r},
\end{equation*}



where the \emph{effective revenue coefficient} is:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-a-eff}]}
A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K) = \frac{[(1-\phi)K]^\alpha}{r - \mu_L + \lambda} + \frac{\lambda}{r - \mu_L + \lambda} \cdot \frac{(\phi K)^\alpha}{r - \mu_H}.
\end{equation*}



\subsubsection*{Option value in regime $H$}

In the absorbing high regime, the option to invest at trigger $X_H^*$ with capacity $K_H^*$ and training fraction $\phi_H^*$ has the standard real-options form (\texttt{dixit1994investment}):

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-option-H}]}
F_H(X) = \left(V_H(X_H^*, K_H^*, \phi_H^*) - I(K_H^*)\right) \left(\frac{X}{X_H^*}\right)^{\beta_H}, \quad X < X_H^*,
\end{equation*}



where $\beta_H > 1$ is the positive root of the H-regime characteristic equation:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-beta-H}]}
\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \beta(\beta - 1) + \mu_H \beta - r = 0.
\end{equation*}



Written as a power function, \texttt{eq-option-H} reads $F_H(X) = B_H X^{\beta_H}$, with $B_H \equiv \left(V_H(X_H^*, K_H^*, \phi_H^*) - I(K_H^*)\right) (X_H^*)^{-\beta_H}$ used below. The optimal trigger satisfies the smooth-pasting condition:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-trigger-H}]}
X_H^* = \frac{\beta_H}{\beta_H - 1} \cdot \frac{(r - \mu_H)}{(\phi K)^{\alpha}} \left(c K^\gamma + \frac{\delta K}{r}\right),
\end{equation*}

so the trigger exceeds the Marshallian (NPV = 0) level by the \emph{option premium} factor $\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1) > 1$, about $2.8$ at baseline.



\subsubsection*{Option value in regime $L$}

In the low regime, the value $F_L$ of a firm that has not yet invested satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation incorporating the regime-switching term:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-hjb-L}]}
\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 X^2 F_L'' + \mu_L X F_L' + \lambda\bigl[F_H(X) - F_L(X)\bigr] - r\, F_L = 0,
\end{equation*}

where $F_H$ is the value the firm holds if the switch arrives before it has invested, not the installed value $V_H$. That value has two branches. Below the H-regime trigger it is the option value $B_H X^{\beta_H}$ of \texttt{eq-option-H.} At or above it the firm invests at once, so $F_H$ is an exercise payoff: $p_H X - q_H$, with $p_H = A_H (K_H^*)^\alpha$ and $q_H = \delta K_H^*/r + I(K_H^*)$, if the scale installed after a switch is precommitted to $K_H^*$, and the envelope $\max_K [A_H K^\alpha X - \delta K/r - I(K)]$ if the firm chooses its scale when the switch arrives. The forcing term in \texttt{eq-hjb-L} is therefore piecewise, and so is the solution.



The homogeneous equation has characteristic equation $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \beta(\beta - 1) + \mu_L \beta - (r + \lambda) = 0$, with roots $\beta_L^+ > 1$ and $\beta_L^- < 0$. Below $X_H^*$ the particular solution has the form $\Gamma \cdot X^{\beta_H}$,

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-particular-C}]}
\Gamma = \frac{-\lambda\, B_H}{Q_L(\beta_H)}, \quad Q_L(\beta) \equiv \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \beta(\beta - 1) + \mu_L \beta - (r + \lambda),
\end{equation*}



and the boundary condition $F_L(0) = 0$ eliminates the negative root:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-option-L-general}]}
F_L(X) = A_1 X^{\beta_L^+} + \Gamma \cdot X^{\beta_H}, \quad X < \min\{X_H^*, X^*\}.
\end{equation*}



Above $X_H^*$, with the post-switch scale precommitted, the forcing is affine and

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-option-L-upper}]}
F_L(X) = G_1 X^{\beta_L^+} + G_2 X^{\beta_L^-} + \frac{\lambda p_H}{r + \lambda - \mu_L}\,X - \frac{\lambda q_H}{r + \lambda}, \quad X_H^* \leq X < X^*.
\end{equation*}

The coefficients $(A_1, G_1, G_2)$ and the trigger $X^*$ are pinned down by value and slope matching at $X_H^*$ and by value matching and smooth pasting at $X^*$. With the envelope in place of the affine payoff the upper branch has no elementary form, and the problem is solved through one scalar equation (Internet Appendix B).



*(i) (Allocation; closed form.) Write $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K) = g(\phi) K^\alpha$, with $g(\phi) = [(1-\phi)^\alpha + \lambda A_H \phi^\alpha]/(r - \mu_L + \lambda)$. At every capacity, installed value in regime $L$ is maximized by the training fraction*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-phi-star}]}
\phi^* = \frac{\rho}{1 + \rho}, \qquad \rho \equiv \left(\frac{\lambda}{r - \mu_H}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}},
\end{equation*}

*which is interior, unique, and independent of $K$; at baseline $\rho \approx 2.34$ and $\phi^* \approx 0.70$. It is increasing in $\lambda$ and in the H-regime growth rate $\mu_H$, and independent of $\mu_L$, which affects inference revenue and the regime-switching discount through the common factor $1/(r - \mu_L + \lambda)$. Because the allocation enters the firm's problem only through $A_{\text{eff}}$, $\phi^*$ is the optimal allocation of any investment made before the switch, whatever the trigger and the capacity.*



*(ii) (Post-switch policy; closed form.) A firm that has not invested when the switch arrives devotes all capacity to training. If demand is then below $X_H^*$, it invests when demand first reaches $X_H^*$ (\texttt{eq-trigger-H} at $\phi = 1$), with capacity*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-K-H}]}
K_H^* = \left[\frac{\delta\,(\alpha \beta_H - \beta_H + 1)}{r\,c\,(\gamma(\beta_H - 1) - \alpha \beta_H)}\right]^{\frac{1}{\gamma - 1}},
\end{equation*}

*the unique global maximizer of the capacity problem, not merely a critical point (Internet Appendix A, Step 4); if demand is already at or above $X_H^*$, it invests at once. At baseline $X_H^* \approx 0.0028$ and $K_H^* \approx 0.0067$.*



*(iii) (Pre-switch policy; a system of conditions.) Let the scale installed after a switch be precommitted to $K_H^*$, so that $F_L$ is given by \texttt{eq-option-L-general} and \texttt{eq-option-L-upper.} An interior pre-switch policy $(X^*, K^*)$ satisfies value matching and smooth pasting at $X^*$ against the payoff $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K^*) X - \delta K^*/r - I(K^*)$, value and slope matching at $X_H^*$, and the scale condition*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-scale-foc}]}
\alpha\, A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K^*)\, X^* = K^* \left(\frac{\delta}{r} + c \gamma (K^*)^{\gamma - 1}\right),
\end{equation*}

*which says that $K^*$ is the capacity a firm investing at demand $X^*$ would choose. When the system returns $X^* < X_H^*$ the upper branch is absent and the scale assumption is immaterial.*



The precommitted scale is a restriction, and removing it changes the answer at baseline. When the firm chooses its scale on arrival of the switch, waiting is worth more at high demand, and whether a finite pre-switch trigger exists is decided by the \emph{waiting margin}

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-waiting-margin}]}
\frac{\lambda}{|Q_L(\theta)|} \left(\frac{A_H}{g(\phi^*)}\right)^{\theta}, \qquad \theta = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma - \alpha},
\end{equation*}

the limiting ratio, as demand grows, of the value of waiting to the payoff from investing at the best scale. If the margin is at least one the firm never invests before the switch. This criterion is derived from the growth rates of the two functions and confirmed by solving the linear complementarity problem; it is not proved. At baseline the margin is $1.08$: the single firm waits for the switch and then follows the post-switch policy of part (ii). A finite pre-switch trigger exists only for arrival rates below about $0.073$ at baseline, and, across the admissible ranges of the other parameters, only at the top of the $\gamma$ range (Internet Appendix B). The amounts at stake are modest. At a demand of half the trigger of \texttt{eq-trigger-phi} below, waiting is worth $1.741 \times 10^{-3}$ against $1.703 \times 10^{-3}$ for following the policy of part (iii), a difference of about $2\%$. The reason for waiting is the one that \texttt{eq-l-insufficiency} describes: once scale can be chosen at the switch, investing earlier buys only the L-regime inference revenue on $(1-\phi)K$, while the H-regime prize is obtained at least as cheaply by waiting. The result rests on the single irreversible lump of the technology: a firm that could expand after entry would not face the same choice.



\subsubsection*{A closed-form approximation}

Replacing the forcing term in \texttt{eq-hjb-L} by $\lambda B_H X^{\beta_H}$ at every demand level and dropping the homogeneous term gives the pure power $F_L(X) \propto X^{\beta_H}$ on the whole continuation region, with its coefficient fixed by value matching. The trigger and capacity are then explicit:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-trigger-phi}]}
X^{\text{pp}} = \frac{\beta_H}{\beta_H - 1} \cdot \frac{\delta K_H^*/r + c(K_H^*)^\gamma}{A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K_H^*)}, \qquad K^{\text{pp}} = K_H^*,
\end{equation*}

which is \texttt{eq-trigger-H} with the H-regime revenue coefficient replaced by the effective one. I call this the \emph{pure-power approximation}. It is a decision rule, not a solution of \texttt{eq-hjb-L}: it pairs a continuation value that solves the H-regime equation with an exercise payoff from the L-regime, its value-matching coefficient is $16.5$ at baseline against the $\Gamma \approx 21.1$ that \texttt{eq-particular-C} requires, and no stopping problem has it as a value function. It is nested in the exact problem in three respects: its allocation is the exact $\phi^*$, its capacity is the post-switch capacity $K_H^*$, and both policies converge to the post-switch policy as $\lambda$ grows without bound. Its measured error at baseline is large in levels and small in value. The trigger $X^{\text{pp}} \approx 0.0047$ is $49\%$ below $X^*$ and the capacity $0.0067$ is $57\%$ below $K^*$, while following the rule delivers $97.4\%$ of the value of the policy of Proposition 1(iii) and $93.1\%$ of the value of waiting (\texttt{tbl-domains}, Internet Appendix B). Two properties of the approximation do not carry over. Its capacity does not depend on beliefs, whereas $K^*$ does; and its trigger falls with the arrival rate over most of the range, whereas the exact trigger does not (Remark 3).



\subsection*{Solution conventions and approximations}

\subsection*{Duopoly with Default Risk}

\subsubsection*{Regime-specific competition}

Revenue in each regime is governed by a Tullock contest success function (\texttt{tullock1980efficient; \texttt{skaperdas1996contest}}) over the regime-relevant capacity measure, so revenue depends on \emph{relative} capacity. In the L-regime, firms compete over \emph{inference capacity}:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-contest-L}]}
\pi_i^L(X, \mathbf{K}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = X \cdot \frac{[(1-\phi_i)K_i]^{2\alpha}}{[(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha + [(1-\phi_j)K_j]^\alpha},
\end{equation*}



which I write equivalently as $\pi_i^L = X \cdot [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha \cdot s_i^L$, where $s_i^L = [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha / \{[(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha + [(1-\phi_j)K_j]^\alpha\}$ is the L-regime contest share. In the H-regime, firms compete over \emph{training compute}:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-contest-H}]}
\pi_i^H(X, \mathbf{K}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = X \cdot \frac{(\phi_i K_i)^{2\alpha}}{(\phi_i K_i)^\alpha + (\phi_j K_j)^\alpha},
\end{equation*}

with H-regime contest share $s_i^H = (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha / \{(\phi_i K_i)^\alpha + (\phi_j K_j)^\alpha\}$.



\subsubsection*{Installed value in the duopoly}

The installed value for firm $i$ in the L-regime combines inference revenue and the expected H-regime continuation:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-duopoly-value-L}]}
V_i^L(X) = A_{\text{eff},i} \cdot X - \frac{\delta K_i}{r},
\end{equation*}



where the effective revenue coefficient for firm $i$ is:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-a-eff-duopoly}]}
A_{\text{eff},i} = \frac{[(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha \cdot s_i^L}{r - \mu_L + \lambda} + \frac{\lambda}{r - \mu_L + \lambda} \cdot \frac{(\phi_i K_i)^\alpha \cdot s_i^H}{r - \mu_H}.
\end{equation*}



\subsubsection*{Capital structure}

\subsubsection*{Default boundary}

Following \texttt{leland1994corporate} and \texttt{leland1996optimal}, equity holders stop funding the firm when equity value reaches zero, and the optimal boundary follows from smooth pasting. For a firm with $(K_i, \phi_i)$ facing a rival with $(K_j, \phi_j)$:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-default-boundary}]}
X_D = \frac{\beta_L^-}{\beta_L^- - 1} \cdot \frac{C_D / r + \delta K_i / r}{A_{\text{eff},i}},
\end{equation*}

where $\beta_L^-$ is the negative root of the L-regime characteristic equation, which incorporates the regime switch through the effective discount rate $r + \lambda$, and $\beta_L^-/(\beta_L^- - 1) \in (0,1)$ is the option value of waiting before defaulting.



*(ii) $X_D$ is decreasing in $\lambda$ precisely when the training allocation is sufficiently high, and the characterization is fully closed-form in the symmetric-shares case ($s_i^L = s_i^H$, as under symmetric capacities\emph{ and }allocations, or monopoly). Two channels operate. The $A_{\text{eff}}$ channel (higher $\lambda$ raises the weight on the H-regime continuation value, lowering $X_D$) is positive if and only if $\phi_i$ exceeds*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-phi-underbar}]}
\underline{\phi} = \frac{\Omega}{1 + \Omega}, \quad \Omega \equiv \left(\frac{r - \mu_H}{r - \mu_L}\right)^{1/\alpha}.
\end{equation*}



*An opposing markup channel operates through the discount root: higher $\lambda$ raises the effective discount rate and pushes $\beta_L^-/(\beta_L^- - 1)$ toward one, raising $X_D$. Because the $A_{\text{eff}}$-channel semi-elasticity is linear in the L-regime flow and H-regime continuation terms, the net condition $\partial X_D / \partial \lambda < 0$ also solves in closed form: it holds if and only if $\phi_i$ exceeds the exact threshold*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-phi-tilde}]}
\tilde{\phi} = \frac{\tilde{\Omega}}{1 + \tilde{\Omega}}, \quad \tilde{\Omega} \equiv \left[\frac{(r - \mu_H)\,(1 + m\Delta)}{(r - \mu_L) - m\lambda\Delta}\right]^{1/\alpha},
\end{equation*}

*where $\Delta = r - \mu_L + \lambda$ and $m = \mathrm{d}\ln M / \mathrm{d}\lambda = 1/[\beta_L^-(\beta_L^- - 1)\mathcal{R}] > 0$ is the markup-channel semi-elasticity, with $\mathcal{R} = \sqrt{(\mu_L - \sigma^2/2)^2 + 2\sigma^2(r+\lambda)}$ (Internet Appendix A states the mild regularity condition). The exact threshold nests $\underline{\phi}$ as the $m \to 0$ limit and satisfies $\tilde{\phi} > \underline{\phi}$. Unlike $\underline{\phi}$, $\tilde{\phi}$ depends on $\lambda$. Finally, $\underline{\phi}$ is increasing in $\alpha$ (with less concavity in the revenue function, a larger training allocation is needed for the H-regime term to dominate), decreasing in $\mu_H - \mu_L$ (a larger regime-switch growth premium amplifies the H-regime term, lowering the threshold), and increasing in $r$ (higher discounting reduces the present value of the continuation opportunity).*



\subsubsection*{Equity and debt values}

Following \texttt{leland1994corporate}, $E(X)$ is the \emph{going-concern} equity value once investment is sunk, and the object relevant for timing is the entry NPV $E(X) - (1-\ell)I(K)$. This is the single equity convention used in the paper, the proofs, and the code: limited liability floors $E$, not the entry NPV. The equity contribution is sunk and is not refunded on default, so the entry NPV is strictly negative at low demand, the boundary condition on which Proposition 3(i) rests. Above the default boundary:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-equity}]}
E(X) = A_{\text{eff},i}\, X - \frac{\delta K}{r} - \frac{C_D}{r} + \left[\frac{C_D}{r} + \frac{\delta K}{r} - A_{\text{eff},i}\, X_D \right]\left(\frac{X}{X_D}\right)^{\beta_L^-},
\end{equation*}

where $\beta_L^- < 0$. The last term is the default option and the bracket the flow deficit at the boundary; value-matching and smooth-pasting on $E$ pin down $X_D$ in \texttt{eq-default-boundary.} At $X = X_D$, $E(X_D) = 0$ and the entry NPV equals $-(1-\ell)I(K) < 0$, as below $X_D$. Without debt, \texttt{eq-equity} at $C_D = 0$ is the \emph{unlevered asset value} $U(X)$, the installed value plus the option to shut down at the shutdown boundary, so equity is continuous in leverage at $\ell = 0$.



Debt value is:

\begin{equation*}
D(X) = \frac{C_D}{r}\left[1 - \left(\frac{X}{X_D}\right)^{\beta_L^-}\right] + R(X_D) \left(\frac{X}{X_D}\right)^{\beta_L^-},
\end{equation*}



where the recovery in default is

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-recovery}]}
R(X_D) = \min\left\{(1 - b)\,\min\left\{\Lambda(X_D),\; U(X_D)\right\},\; \frac{C_D}{r}\right\},
\end{equation*}



where

\begin{equation*}
\Lambda(X) = \begin{cases} a_i X - c_i + (c_i - a_i X_I)\left(\dfrac{X}{X_I}\right)^{\beta_L^-} & X > X_I, \\ 0 & X \leq X_I, \end{cases}
\end{equation*}

with $a_i = [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha s_i^L/(r - \mu_L + \lambda)$ the inference revenue coefficient, $c_i = \delta(1-\phi_i)K_i/r$ the operating cost of the inference capacity, and $X_I = [\beta_L^-/(\beta_L^- - 1)]\, c_i/a_i$. Here $b \in [0,1]$ is the fraction of liquidation value lost in bankruptcy and $\Lambda(X_D)$ the liquidation value of productive assets. Only the \emph{inference} business survives liquidation, while the H-regime continuation value is destroyed, because the post-AGI payoff requires the going concern. The liquidation value is that of the inference business to an owner who carries the same perpetual cost $\delta$ per unit of capacity as the firm, which is the cost that brings the firm to $X_D$ in the first place, and who, like the unlevered firm, may shut the business down: $X_I$ is \texttt{eq-default-boundary} applied to the inference business alone at a zero coupon, and $\Lambda$ is that business's unlevered asset value in the same single-boundary form as $U$. As in \texttt{leland1994corporate}, what creditors take over is an asset value. Without the option term, $a_i X - c_i$ plus the training business is exactly the installed value \texttt{eq-installed-value-L.} Recovery is capped twice: by the unlevered asset value $U(X_D)$ of the assets seized, because a small inference capacity can be worth more than a whole firm that cannot shed its training capacity, and by the default-free value of the claim.



\subsubsection*{Entry equilibrium}

\textbf{First investment and rent equalization.} Both firms share the same $\lambda$ and the game is symmetric; cross-sectional variation in investment behavior (\texttt{sec-calibration}, \texttt{sec-valuation}) comes from comparative statics across archetypes, not from interaction among firms with different priors. What a firm is worth before either has invested depends on what happens if the switch arrives first. Let $W(X)$ be the value to each firm when neither invests before the switch. At the switch the two firms play the entry game of the absorbing regime, which is a preemption race, so that each is worth the follower's value in it (Internet Appendix B). A firm that leads at a trigger $\bar{X}$, its rival never investing first, is worth $W(X) + [L^*(\bar{X}) - W(\bar{X})](X/\bar{X})^{\beta_L^+}$ below it, and $X_L$ is the trigger that maximizes this value:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-first-investment}]}
X_L = \arg\max_{X}\; \bigl[L^*(X) - W(X)\bigr]\,X^{-\beta_L^+}.
\end{equation*}

The rent-equalization trigger $X_P$ is the lowest demand level at which $L^*(X) = F(X)$, with $F$ the follower's value against the policy the leader chooses at $X$. Above it each firm would rather lead than follow, so the first investment cannot come later. In the standard preemption game $X_P < X_L$: leading is the better role at the leader's own trigger, the two firms race, and entry is brought forward to $X_P$, where the rent from leading is dissipated. When instead $X_L < X_P$, following is the better role at $X_L$, and a firm gains nothing by investing ahead of a rival that will lead there. The strategies in which one firm leads at $X_L$ and the other follows then form an equilibrium if two conditions hold. The leader must prefer $X_L$ to every other stopping rule, given that its rival never invests first. The follower must prefer waiting to investing first at every demand level below $X_L$, where its value is that of waiting for the leader's entry or for the switch, $W(X) + [F(X_L) - W(X_L)](X/X_L)^{\beta_L^+}$, and not $F(X)$. That value exceeds the leader's whenever $F(X_L) \geq L^*(X_L)$, so the second condition follows from the first whenever $X_L \leq X_P$. Proposition 3(iii) reports that this is the case on the whole grid.



*(i) (Analytical; the follower after the switch, for the claim without the option to stop) Against a leader with training capacity $T_L = \phi_L K_L$, a follower that has not invested when the switch arrives devotes all capacity to training, installs the capacity $K_F$ that solves*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-follower-foc}]}
\alpha \beta_H \bigl(2 - s_F(K)\bigr)\,\Theta(K) = (\beta_H - 1)\,K\,\Theta'(K), \qquad s_F(K) = \frac{K^\alpha}{K^\alpha + T_L^\alpha}, \quad \Theta(K) = \frac{\delta K}{r} + I(K),
\end{equation*}

*and enters at $X_F^* = [\beta_H/(\beta_H - 1)]\,\Theta(K_F)/[A_H K_F^\alpha s_F(K_F)]$. The solution is unique whenever $(\beta_H - 1)/(2\alpha\beta_H) < 1$ and $(\beta_H - 1)/(\alpha\beta_H) > 1/\gamma$, the second of which is the lower bound of (A2). The follower's marginal revenue elasticity is $\alpha(2 - s_F)$ where the single firm's is $\alpha$, and at baseline the follower builds far more than the single firm and enters later. With the option to stop, $K_F$ and $X_F^*$ are computed numerically and differ from these by less than $0.2\%$ at baseline.*

\subsubsection*{Setup}

\subsubsection*{Value Loss}

The value loss from mismatch is

\begin{equation*}
\Delta V = \text{NPV}(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{true}}) - \text{NPV}(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{invest}}),
\end{equation*}

where $\text{NPV}(\lambda_a, \lambda_b)$ is the expected present value, at a common initial demand level $X_0$, of the policy $(X^*, K^*, \phi^*)$ optimal for belief $\lambda_b$ when the true demand process is governed by $\lambda_a$, with the timing discount $(X_0/X^*)^{\beta_H}$ adjusting for different waiting times. Percentage losses are reported as $\Delta V / \text{NPV}(\lambda_{\text{true}}, \lambda_{\text{true}})$. The levered version keeps the same operating policy and changes only the claim being valued: $\text{NPV}$ then denotes the total claims net of the investment outlay, $E + D - I(K^*)$ with $E$ the going-concern equity of \texttt{sec-duopoly.} Because that policy is not re-optimized against the levered objective, the levered value function is maximized very nearly, but not exactly, at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = \lambda_{\text{true}}$; the resulting shortfall is three orders of magnitude below the mismatch losses reported here (Internet Appendix A).

\subsection*{A. Proofs and Supporting Derivations}

\subsubsection*{Proof of Proposition 1}

\emph{Step 1: Optimal trigger given capacity.} Steps 1--4 solve a stopping problem with exercise payoff $a K^\alpha X - \Theta(K)$, where $a > 0$ does not depend on $K$, $\Theta(K) = cK^\gamma + \delta K / r$ is the investment outlay plus the present value of the operating-cost flow, and the continuation value is the single power $B X^{\beta_H}$. With $a = A_H$ this is the absorbing H-regime problem of a firm that devotes all capacity to training, which is optimal there because inference capacity earns nothing after the switch. Value matching and smooth pasting yield:

\begin{equation*}
X(K) = \frac{\beta_H}{\beta_H - 1} \cdot \frac{\Theta(K)}{a K^\alpha}.
\end{equation*}



\emph{Step 2: NPV at the trigger.} The present value of revenue at the trigger is $a K^\alpha X(K) = \frac{\beta_H}{\beta_H - 1} \Theta(K)$, so the NPV at the trigger is:

\begin{equation*}
V - I = \frac{1}{\beta_H - 1}\, \Theta(K).
\end{equation*}



\emph{Step 3: Reduced capacity objective.} Substituting the trigger and NPV into the option value $F(X_0) = (V - I)(X_0/X(K))^{\beta_H}$:

\begin{equation*}
F(X_0) = \mathcal{C} \cdot \frac{(a K^\alpha)^{\beta_H}}{\Theta(K)^{\beta_H - 1}} \equiv \mathcal{C} \cdot h(K),
\end{equation*}

where $\mathcal{C} = \frac{1}{\beta_H - 1}\left(\frac{(\beta_H - 1) X_0}{\beta_H}\right)^{\beta_H} > 0$ is independent of $K$. The optimal capacity maximizes $h(K)$.



*Step 4: First-order condition for $K$.* Setting $(\partial \ln h / \partial K) = 0$:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-foc-K}]}
\frac{\alpha \beta_H}{K} = \frac{(\beta_H - 1)(c\gamma K^{\gamma - 1} + \delta / r)}{cK^\gamma + \delta K / r}.
\end{equation*}

The coefficient $a$ has dropped out, so the solution depends only on the cost and technology parameters $(\alpha, \beta_H, \gamma, \delta, r, c)$. Solving for $K$ yields the closed form \texttt{eq-K-H.} The critical point is the global maximum. The function $h \propto K^{\alpha\beta_H} / (cK^\gamma + \delta K/r)^{\beta_H - 1}$ is continuous and strictly positive on $(0, \infty)$. As $K \to 0$ the linear term dominates the denominator and $h \sim K^{\alpha\beta_H - (\beta_H - 1)} \to 0$, because the upper bound in (A2) gives $\alpha\beta_H > \beta_H - 1$. As $K \to \infty$ the convex term dominates and $h \sim K^{\alpha\beta_H - \gamma(\beta_H - 1)} \to 0$, because the lower bound in (A2) gives $\alpha\beta_H < \gamma(\beta_H - 1)$. A positive continuous function vanishing at both ends attains an interior maximum, and \texttt{eq-foc-K} is linear in $K^{\gamma - 1}$ with a single root, so that root is it. Both limits require $\delta > 0$: at $\delta = 0$ the denominator is $cK^\gamma$ alone, $h \sim K^{\alpha\beta_H - \gamma(\beta_H - 1)}$ is monotonically decreasing on the whole half-line, and no interior optimum exists (the closed form returns zero), which is why (A1) imposes $\delta > 0$. The same four steps with $a = g(\phi)$, the coefficient of $A_{\text{eff}} = g(\phi) K^\alpha$, are the pure-power approximation of \texttt{sec-single-firm}, which is why its capacity is $K_H^*$ whatever the allocation and the arrival rate, and why its trigger \texttt{eq-trigger-phi} is $X_H^* A_H / g(\phi^*)$.



The first derivative with respect to $\phi$ is:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial A_{\text{eff}}}{\partial \phi} = \alpha K^\alpha \bigl[-w_L (1-\phi)^{\alpha - 1} + w_H \phi^{\alpha - 1}\bigr].
\end{equation*}



\emph{Uniqueness.} The second derivative is:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^2 A_{\text{eff}}}{\partial \phi^2} = \alpha(\alpha - 1) K^\alpha \bigl[w_L (1-\phi)^{\alpha - 2} + w_H \phi^{\alpha - 2}\bigr] < 0
\end{equation*}

for all $\phi \in (0,1)$, since $\alpha \in (0,1)$ implies $\alpha(\alpha-1) < 0$ while both bracketed terms $(1-\phi)^{\alpha - 2}$ and $\phi^{\alpha - 2}$ are positive. Strict concavity of $A_{\text{eff}}$ in $\phi$ guarantees uniqueness.



\emph{Interior solution.} Setting $\partial A_{\text{eff}} / \partial \phi = 0$ yields:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{w_H}{w_L} = \left(\frac{1-\phi^*}{\phi^*}\right)^{\alpha - 1},
\end{equation*}

which uniquely determines $\phi^*$ as an increasing function of $w_H / w_L$.



\emph{Step 7: The pre-switch policy with precommitted post-switch scale.} Let $S(X)$ denote the value of never investing before the switch and installing $K_H^*$ after it. It solves \texttt{eq-hjb-L} on the whole half-line: $S(X) = A_w X^{\beta_L^+} + \Gamma X^{\beta_H}$ below $X_H^*$ and $S(X) = G_w X^{\beta_L^-} + [\lambda p_H/(r + \lambda - \mu_L)] X - \lambda q_H/(r + \lambda)$ above it, where the no-bubble condition removes $X^{\beta_L^+}$ from the upper branch and $(A_w, G_w)$ are pinned by value and slope matching at $X_H^*$. Consider the policy of installing $(K, \phi^*)$ when demand first reaches $\bar{X}$, with payoff $P(X; K) = g(\phi^*) K^\alpha X - \Theta(K)$. Below $\bar{X}$ its value differs from $S$ by a solution of the homogeneous equation that vanishes at the origin, so

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-premium}]}
F_L(X) = S(X) + \bigl[P(\bar{X}; K) - S(\bar{X})\bigr] \left(\frac{X}{\bar{X}}\right)^{\beta_L^+}, \quad X < \bar{X}.
\end{equation*}

The firm maximizes the coefficient $[P(\bar{X}; K) - S(\bar{X})]\,\bar{X}^{-\beta_L^+}$, which does not depend on the demand level at which it stands. The first-order condition in $\bar{X}$ is $\bar{X}\,[g(\phi^*) K^\alpha - S'(\bar{X})] = \beta_L^+ [P(\bar{X}; K) - S(\bar{X})]$, which is smooth pasting of \texttt{eq-premium} against the payoff, value matching holding by construction. The first-order condition in $K$ is $\partial P / \partial K = 0$ at $\bar{X}$, which is \texttt{eq-scale-foc.} Writing out \texttt{eq-premium} on the two sides of $X_H^*$ gives \texttt{eq-option-L-general} with $A_1 = A_w + [P - S]\,\bar{X}^{-\beta_L^+}$ and \texttt{eq-option-L-upper} with $G_1 = [P - S]\,\bar{X}^{-\beta_L^+}$ and $G_2 = G_w$, and the value and slope matching at $X_H^*$ is inherited from $S$. These are the conditions of part (iii). They are necessary for an interior optimum; that the coefficient has a single maximum in $K$ is verified numerically (Internet Appendix B), not proved. At baseline $A_w \approx -1.18 \times 10^4$ and $A_1 \approx -0.85 \times 10^4$. $\square$



\emph{The approximation.} Imposing $A_1 = 0$ and pricing the pre-investment option with the pure power form $F_L(X) \propto X^{\beta_H}$ on the whole continuation region gives the pure-power approximation. It is the unconditional-$A_{\text{eff}}$ convention of \texttt{sec-conventions} applied to the single firm: option-like L-regime payoffs are discounted with the H-regime exponent $\beta_H$ in place of a regime-switching first-passage factor mixing $X^{\beta_L^+}$ and $X^{\beta_H}$, and the exercise payoff is the unconditional L-regime installed value. With a single power in the continuation region, dividing value-matching by smooth pasting at the trigger eliminates the coefficient and yields:

\begin{equation*}
X^{\text{pp}} = \frac{\beta_H}{\beta_H - 1} \cdot \frac{\delta K_H^*/r + I(K_H^*)}{A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K_H^*)},
\end{equation*}

which is \texttt{eq-trigger-phi} (Steps 1--4 with $a = g(\phi^*)$). The trigger depends only on the value-matching/smooth-pasting ratio, not on the level of the coefficient, which value-matching then determines; the two boundary conditions pin down the trigger and the level jointly. The price is that this smooth-fit level differs from the forced-ODE value $\Gamma$ of \texttt{eq-particular-C}: at the baseline calibration the smooth-fit coefficient is $[V(X^{\text{pp}}, K_H^*, \phi^*) - I(K_H^*)]/(X^{\text{pp}})^{\beta_H} \approx 16.5$ against $\Gamma \approx 21.1$, so the candidate does not solve \texttt{eq-hjb-L} on any interval and is a decision rule, not a value function. The direction of the resulting error is not implied by that comparison; Internet Appendix B measures it against the exact solution. At the baseline calibration and at the approximate policy, the precommitted-scale continuation value exceeds the smooth-fit value at every demand level while remaining below $\Gamma X^{\beta_H}$, so the approximation understates the pre-investment option value, by 19\\% at $X_0 = X^{\text{pp}}/2$. The ordering is not general: it reverses for $\lambda \leq 0.02$. The comparison shows what the approximation preserves and what it does not. Its levels $X^{\text{pp}}$ and $K^{\text{pp}}$ are not estimates of the exact policy, whose trigger and capacity are about twice as large. The training fraction $\phi^*$ is identical in the two. And the value delivered by the approximate policy is within about 3\\% of the value of the exact policy of Proposition 1(iii) and within about 7\\% of the unrestricted optimum, which at baseline is to wait for the switch (Internet Appendix B).



\subsubsection*{Proof of Proposition 2}

The approximation is to replace $E_H$ with its perpetuity component:

\begin{equation*}
E_H(X) \approx A_H (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha \cdot s_i^H \cdot X - C_D/r - \delta K_i/r,
\end{equation*}

after which the L-regime equity ODE yields a particular solution with coefficient $A_{\text{eff},i}$, and Leland's smooth pasting gives the default boundary below in closed form. The omitted term $D_H X^{\beta_H^-}$ is the (positive) value of the H-regime default option, so the perpetuity approximation understates the H-regime continuation value and the closed-form boundary weakly \emph{overstates} $X_D$. The magnitude of the bias is computed by solving the coupled system exactly: substituting the closed-form $E_H$ (including $D_H X^{\beta_H^-}$) into the L-regime ODE yields an additional particular term $C_2 X^{\beta_H^-}$ with $C_2 = -\lambda D_H / Q_L(\beta_H^-)$, and value matching plus smooth pasting at $X_D$ then determine the boundary jointly with the homogeneous coefficient. At the baseline calibration the closed-form boundary exceeds the coupled-system boundary by approximately 3\\%, uniformly across leverage levels (Internet Appendix B). The approximation therefore errs against the faith-based survival mechanism, making the levered firm look slightly riskier than the coupled system implies, and is conservative for the credit-risk conclusions.



In the L-regime, the going-concern equity $E(X)$ of \texttt{eq-equity} satisfies an ODE analogous to \texttt{eq-hjb-L}, with the firm defaulting when $E(X_D) = 0$ and $E'(X_D) = 0$ (smooth pasting); the sunk equity contribution enters the entry NPV $E(X) - (1-\ell)I(K)$ but not the boundary conditions. The resulting default boundary is:

\begin{equation*}
X_D = \frac{\beta_L^-}{\beta_L^- - 1} \cdot \frac{C_D/r + \delta K_i/r}{A_{\text{eff},i}},
\end{equation*}

where $\beta_L^-$ is the negative characteristic root, $C_D = r_c \cdot \ell \cdot I(K)$ is the coupon, and all comparative statics below hold *with $(K_i, \phi_i)$ and $(K_j, \phi_j)$ held fixed*. Nothing in the derivation requires $C_D > 0$: at $\ell = 0$ the same value-matching and smooth-pasting conditions, applied to the unlevered claim, give the shutdown boundary $[\beta_L^-/(\beta_L^- - 1)]\,(\delta K_i/r)/A_{\text{eff},i}$, which is positive under (A1). Parts (ii) to (iv) therefore hold for $\ell \geq 0$, and so does part (i) in $\ell$.



*(ii) Default boundary decreasing in $\lambda$ (faith-based survival).* Holding $(K_i, \phi_i, K_j, \phi_j)$ fixed, define the L-regime revenue flow $\Pi_L \equiv [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha \cdot s_i^L$ and the H-regime revenue present value $\Pi_H \equiv (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha \cdot s_i^H / (r - \mu_H)$, both positive. The effective revenue coefficient is:

\begin{equation*}
A_{\text{eff},i} = \frac{\Pi_L + \lambda \cdot \Pi_H}{r - \mu_L + \lambda}.
\end{equation*}



Differentiating with respect to $\lambda$:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial A_{\text{eff},i}}{\partial \lambda} = \frac{\Pi_H(r - \mu_L) - \Pi_L}{(r - \mu_L + \lambda)^2}.
\end{equation*}



This is positive whenever $\Pi_H(r - \mu_L) > \Pi_L$, i.e., when the H-regime revenue present value scaled by the L-regime net discount rate $r - \mu_L$ exceeds the L-regime revenue flow:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-faith-condition}]}
\frac{(\phi_i K_i)^\alpha \cdot s_i^H}{r - \mu_H} \cdot (r - \mu_L) > [(1-\phi_i)K_i]^\alpha \cdot s_i^L.
\end{equation*}

Since $\mu_H > \mu_L$ implies $(r - \mu_L)/(r - \mu_H) > 1$, the factor $(r - \mu_L)$ amplifies the H-regime term, making the condition easier to satisfy. Intuitively, the condition requires that the training fraction $\phi_i$ is large enough that the H-regime continuation value contributes meaningfully to $A_{\text{eff},i}$.



\emph{Closed-form threshold (symmetric duopoly).} In the symmetric case with $s_i^L = s_i^H = 1/2$ and equal capacity, the contest shares and $K^\alpha$ terms cancel, and the condition reduces to $(r - \mu_L)/(r - \mu_H) \cdot \phi^\alpha > (1-\phi)^\alpha$, i.e., $(\phi/(1-\phi))^\alpha > (r-\mu_H)/(r-\mu_L)$. Solving for $\phi$:

\begin{equation*}
\phi > \underline{\phi} = \frac{\Omega}{1 + \Omega}, \quad \Omega = \left(\frac{r - \mu_H}{r - \mu_L}\right)^{1/\alpha}.
\end{equation*}

For the baseline calibration ($r = 0.12$, $\mu_H = 0.06$, $\mu_L = 0.01$, $\alpha = 0.40$): $\Omega = (0.06/0.11)^{2.5} \approx 0.22$, giving $\underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$.



\emph{Markup channel.} To complete the proof, note that $X_D$ also depends on $\lambda$ through the markup factor $M(\beta_L^-) \equiv \beta_L^- / (\beta_L^- - 1)$, since $\beta_L^-$ is the negative root of $\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \beta(\beta - 1) + \mu_L \beta - (r + \lambda) = 0$ and thus depends on $\lambda$. The full derivative decomposes into two opposing channels:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial X_D}{\partial \lambda} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial M}{\partial \lambda} \cdot \frac{N}{A_{\text{eff},i}}}_{>0\;\text{($\beta$-channel)}} + \underbrace{M(\beta_L^-) \cdot N \cdot \frac{\partial (1/A_{\text{eff},i})}{\partial \lambda}}_{<0\;\text{($A_{\text{eff}}$-channel)}},
\end{equation*}

where $N = C_D/r + \delta K_i/r > 0$. The $\beta$-channel is positive because increasing $\lambda$ raises the hazard-adjusted discount rate $(r + \lambda)$, making $\beta_L^-$ more negative and pushing the markup $M$ toward 1 from below (since $\beta_L^- < 0$ implies $M \in (0,1)$): $dM/d\lambda = 1/[(\beta_L^- - 1)^2 \mathcal{R}] > 0$, where $\mathcal{R} = \sqrt{(\mu_L - \sigma^2/2)^2 + 2\sigma^2(r+\lambda)}$ is the discriminant of the L-regime characteristic equation. The $A_{\text{eff}}$-channel is negative under \texttt{eq-faith-condition.}



\emph{Exact net threshold.} The net sign resolves in closed form. In log form, $\partial \ln X_D / \partial \lambda = m - \partial \ln A_{\text{eff},i} / \partial \lambda$, where the markup semi-elasticity is $m \equiv (\mathrm{d}M/\mathrm{d}\lambda)/M = 1/[\beta_L^-(\beta_L^- - 1)\mathcal{R}] > 0$, and, from the derivative above,

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \ln A_{\text{eff},i}}{\partial \lambda} = \frac{\Pi_H(r - \mu_L) - \Pi_L}{(\Pi_L + \lambda \Pi_H)\,\Delta}, \qquad \Delta \equiv r - \mu_L + \lambda,
\end{equation*}



with $\Delta$ the hazard-adjusted net discount rate of the L-regime. The condition $\partial X_D / \partial \lambda < 0$ is therefore $\Pi_H(r - \mu_L) - \Pi_L > m(\Pi_L + \lambda \Pi_H)\Delta$, which is \emph{linear} in $(\Pi_L, \Pi_H)$ and rearranges to

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\Pi_H}{\Pi_L} > \frac{1 + m\Delta}{(r - \mu_L) - m\lambda\Delta},
\end{equation*}

provided the regularity condition $(r - \mu_L) > m\lambda\Delta$ holds (it does throughout the calibration ranges; if it fails, no allocation can deliver $\partial X_D/\partial\lambda < 0$). With symmetric shares, $\Pi_H/\Pi_L = (\phi/(1-\phi))^\alpha / (r - \mu_H)$, giving the exact threshold $\tilde{\phi}$ of \texttt{eq-phi-tilde.} Since $m > 0$, $\tilde{\Omega} > \Omega$ and $\tilde{\phi} > \underline{\phi}$; as $m \to 0$ (no markup channel), $\tilde{\phi} \to \underline{\phi}$. At the baseline calibration $m \approx 0.77$ and $\tilde{\phi} \approx 0.32$, between $\underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$ and $\phi^* \approx 0.70$; the numerically measured $\beta$-channel is about one-third of the $A_{\text{eff}}$-channel at $\phi^*$, consistent with the closed form. The sign flip of $\partial X_D/\partial \lambda$ at $\tilde{\phi}$ is verified by finite differences.



\subsubsection*{Installed value in the arrival rate (Corollary 1)}

\textbf{Corollary 1} (Installed value in $\lambda$). *Hold a single installed firm's capacity $K > 0$, allocation $\phi \in (0, 1)$, coupon $C_D \geq 0$ and current demand $X > 0$ fixed, and let $\lambda \geq 0$ vary, with $\Pi_L = [(1-\phi)K]^\alpha$, $\Pi_H = (\phi K)^\alpha/(r - \mu_H)$, $\Delta = r - \mu_L + \lambda$ and $G \equiv \Pi_H (r - \mu_L) - \Pi_L$. The going-concern value $V(\lambda) = A_{\text{eff}}(\lambda) X - (\delta K + C_D)/r$, the installed value of \texttt{eq-installed-value-L} net of the default-free coupon claim and without the option to stop, satisfies*

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-installed-lambda}]}
V'(\lambda) = \frac{X G}{\Delta^2}, \qquad V''(\lambda) = -\frac{2 X G}{\Delta^3}.
\end{equation*}

*(i) $V$ is strictly increasing and strictly concave in $\lambda$ on all of $\lambda \geq 0$ if and only if $\phi > \underline{\phi}$ of \texttt{eq-phi-underbar}; it is strictly decreasing and strictly convex if $\phi < \underline{\phi}$ and constant at $\phi = \underline{\phi}$. (ii) For news of size $h \in (0, \Delta)$, $[V(\lambda) - V(\lambda - h)] - [V(\lambda + h) - V(\lambda)] = 2h^2 X G/[\Delta(\Delta - h)(\Delta + h)]$, which is positive if and only if $\phi > \underline{\phi}$: bad news lowers value by more than good news of the same size raises it. (iii) At given $(\lambda, K, X)$, $V'$, $|V''|$ and the difference in (ii) increase in $\phi$, and so does the semi-elasticity of the revenue value $A_{\text{eff}} X$ in $\lambda$.*



\subsubsection*{Proof of Proposition 3}

\emph{Part (i): the follower after the switch (analytical).} After the switch the regime is absorbing and the leader's capacity is installed, so no decision of the leader remains and the follower faces a standard investment problem under a geometric Brownian motion with drift $\mu_H$. Inference capacity earns nothing after the switch, so any $\phi_F < 1$ is dominated and the follower trains with all its capacity. Entering at demand $X$ with capacity $K$ then pays $a(K)X - \Theta(K)$, with $a(K) = A_H K^{2\alpha}/(K^\alpha + T_L^\alpha) = A_H K^\alpha s_F(K)$ the revenue coefficient of \texttt{eq-contest-H} and $\Theta(K) = \delta K/r + I(K)$. For a given $K$ this is the problem of Step 1 of the Proof of Proposition 1: the trigger is $[\beta_H/(\beta_H-1)]\,\Theta(K)/a(K)$ and the option coefficient is proportional to $a(K)^{\beta_H}/\Theta(K)^{\beta_H - 1}$. Its logarithmic derivative with respect to $\ln K$ is

\begin{equation*}
\beta_H\,\alpha\,\bigl(2 - s_F(K)\bigr) - (\beta_H - 1)\,\frac{K\Theta'(K)}{\Theta(K)},
\end{equation*}

because $\mathrm{d}\ln a/\mathrm{d}\ln K = \alpha(2 - s_F)$. The share $s_F$ is increasing in $K$ and $K\Theta'/\Theta = (\delta K/r + \gamma c K^\gamma)/(\delta K/r + cK^\gamma)$ rises from $1$ to $\gamma$, so the derivative is strictly decreasing in $K$. It is positive as $K \to 0$ if and only if $2\alpha\beta_H > \beta_H - 1$ and negative as $K \to \infty$ if and only if $\alpha\beta_H < \gamma(\beta_H - 1)$, which are the two conditions of the statement. The coefficient therefore has a unique interior maximizer, the root of \texttt{eq-follower-foc.} With $T_L = 0$ the share is one and the condition is \texttt{eq-foc-K}, the single firm's post-switch problem of Proposition 1(ii); the small-capacity condition is weaker than the upper bound of (A2) because the follower's small-capacity elasticity is $2\alpha$.



\emph{Part (ii): allocation (analytical critical point; equilibrium allocation numerical).} Consider a firm that enters before the switch against an installed rival. Once both firms are installed no decision remains, so its installed value is $A_{\text{eff},i}X - \delta K_i/r$ with $A_{\text{eff},i}$ given by \texttt{eq-a-eff-duopoly}, exactly, for the claim that operates forever. Write the Tullock contest payoff over the regime-relevant capacity measure $u$ (with rival measure $\bar{u}$ fixed) as $f(u) = u^{2\alpha} / (u^\alpha + \bar{u}^\alpha)$. Differentiating,

\begin{equation*}
f'(u) = \alpha\, u^{\alpha - 1}\, s\,(2 - s), \qquad s = \frac{u^\alpha}{u^\alpha + \bar{u}^\alpha}:
\end{equation*}



the marginal contest revenue is the standalone marginal revenue $\alpha u^{\alpha-1}$ scaled by the common multiplier $s(2-s)$. When the two firms have the same training fraction $\phi$, the regime-relevant capacity ratios coincide across regimes ($u/\bar{u} = K_i/K_j$ for inference and training alike), so the share $s$, and hence the multiplier, is the same in the L-regime and H-regime terms of the allocation condition:

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial A_{\text{eff},i}}{\partial \phi_i}\bigg|_{\phi_i = \phi_j = \phi} = \alpha K_i^\alpha\, s\,(2 - s)\,\bigl[-w_L (1-\phi)^{\alpha-1} + w_H \phi^{\alpha-1}\bigr].
\end{equation*}

The multiplier cancels, leaving the single-firm condition of Proposition 1, Step 5, whose unique zero is $\phi^*$. Hence, for any capacity pair, a common allocation $\phi$ is a critical point of the entrant's allocation problem if and only if $\phi = \phi^*$: against a rival at $\phi^*$ the entrant's allocation condition is the single firm's. That the critical point is a maximum, and the allocation against a rival away from $\phi^*$, are not characterized analytically.



\emph{Values before the first investment.} Until the leader invests nothing is paid, so for $X < X_L$ both values solve the L-regime equation with $\lambda$ times the post-switch value as forcing. They are therefore $W$ plus a multiple of $X^{\beta_L^+}$, pinned by the payoffs at $X_L$:

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-values-before-entry}]}
V_{\text{lead}}(X) = W(X) + \bigl[L^*(X_L) - W(X_L)\bigr]\Bigl(\frac{X}{X_L}\Bigr)^{\beta_L^+}, \qquad V_{\text{follow}}(X) = W(X) + \bigl[F(X_L) - W(X_L)\bigr]\Bigl(\frac{X}{X_L}\Bigr)^{\beta_L^+},
\end{equation*}

with $F(X_L)$ the follower's value against the policy the leader installs at $X_L$. The follower's value before the leader's entry is $V_{\text{follow}}$, the value of waiting for that entry or for the switch. It is not $F(X)$, which is what the follower would be worth if the leader invested at $X$.



\subsubsection*{Numerical Finding 1 (Dario's dilemma)}

\subsection*{B. Numerical Verification Methods}

\emph{Installed value by discounted expectation.} Both \texttt{eq-installed-value-H} and \texttt{eq-installed-value-L} are special cases of the same construction: the value of installed capacity is the expected discounted flow of revenue net of the operating cost, $V = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\int_0^\infty e^{-rt} \bigl(\pi_t - \delta K\bigr)\, dt\bigr]$, under the risk-adjusted discounting convention documented later in this appendix. In the absorbing H-regime, flow revenue is $\pi_t = X_t (\phi K)^\alpha$ with $X_t$ a GBM of drift $\mu_H$, so $\mathbb{E}[X_t] = X_0 e^{\mu_H t}$ and

\begin{equation*}
\mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^\infty e^{-rt} X_t\, dt\right] (\phi K)^\alpha = (\phi K)^\alpha \int_0^\infty e^{-(r-\mu_H)t} X_0\, dt = \frac{X_0 (\phi K)^\alpha}{r - \mu_H},
\end{equation*}

which is finite because (A1) requires $r > \mu_H$; the operating-cost flow contributes $-\delta K \int_0^\infty e^{-rt}\, dt = -\delta K/r$, and summing the two terms gives \texttt{eq-installed-value-H.} In the L-regime the regime switch arrives at rate $\lambda$ and is absorbing, so before the switch $X_t$ has drift $\mu_L$ and the switch time $\tau$ is exponential with parameter $\lambda$, independent of the driving Brownian motion. Splitting the integral at $\tau$ and using the expectation over the exponential switch time $\tau$ to integrate out the random switch time gives the effective discount rate $r - \mu_L + \lambda$ on the pre-switch inference flow, and the term $\lambda/(r - \mu_L + \lambda)$ multiplying the post-switch training value $A_H X (\phi K)^\alpha$: this is exactly the two terms of \texttt{eq-a-eff}, with the second term the Laplace transform of the exponential switching time evaluated at the L-regime net discount rate. When the model is extended to the duopoly, the same construction applies with flow revenue replaced by the contest-weighted flows $\pi_i^L(X, \mathbf{K}, \boldsymbol\phi)$ and $\pi_i^H(X, \mathbf{K}, \boldsymbol\phi)$ of \texttt{eq-contest-L} and \texttt{eq-contest-H}, holding rival capacity and allocation fixed: because the contest shares $s_i^L$ and $s_i^H$ do not depend on $X$, they factor out of the expectation exactly as $(\phi K)^\alpha$ does in the single-firm case, giving \texttt{eq-a-eff-duopoly} and $V_i^H(X) = A_H X (\phi_i K_i)^\alpha s_i^H - \delta K_i/r$ with no change to the discounting argument.



\emph{Smooth pasting for the H-regime trigger.} \texttt{eq-trigger-H} follows from the two standard boundary conditions on the option value $F_H(X) = B_H X^{\beta_H}$ at the unknown trigger $X_H^*$: value matching, $B_H (X_H^*)^{\beta_H} = V_H(X_H^*, K, \phi) - I(K)$, equates the option value to the net payoff from exercising, and smooth pasting, $\beta_H B_H (X_H^*)^{\beta_H - 1} = \partial V_H/\partial X = A_H(\phi K)^\alpha$, equates the slopes so that the free boundary is chosen optimally rather than arbitrarily. Dividing smooth pasting by value matching eliminates the unknown coefficient $B_H$ and leaves one equation in $X_H^*$,

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\beta_H}{X_H^*} = \frac{A_H (\phi K)^\alpha}{A_H (\phi K)^\alpha X_H^* - \delta K/r - cK^\gamma},
\end{equation*}

which rearranges to \texttt{eq-trigger-H} once $A_H (\phi K)^\alpha X_H^*$ is isolated on one side; back-substituting into value matching then gives $B_H$. The same two conditions, applied to $F_L(X) \propto X^{\beta_H}$ and to $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi^*, K^*)$ in place of $A_H(\phi K)^\alpha$, give the pure-power trigger \texttt{eq-trigger-phi} by the identical algebra, which is why the two triggers share the option-premium factor $\beta_H/(\beta_H-1)$.



\emph{Claims before the switch.} Fix the leader's policy $(K_L, \phi_L)$ and write $T_L = \phi_L K_L$ and $N_L = (1-\phi_L)K_L$ for its training and inference capacity. Every claim $V$ held in regime $L$ solves

\begin{equation*}
\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 X^2 V'' + \mu_L X V' - (r + \lambda)V + f(X) = 0,
\end{equation*}



with $f$ its flow plus $\lambda$ times its value at a switch. The solution that is bounded at the origin and free of the explosive root is

\begin{equation*}
\tag*{[\texttt{eq-green}]}
P(X) = \frac{2}{\sigma^2(\beta_L^+ - \beta_L^-)}\left[X^{\beta_L^-}\int_0^X f(y)\,y^{-\beta_L^- - 1}\,\mathrm{d}y + X^{\beta_L^+}\int_X^\infty f(y)\,y^{-\beta_L^+ - 1}\,\mathrm{d}y\right],
\end{equation*}

to which multiples of $X^{\beta_L^-}$ and $X^{\beta_L^+}$ are added as boundary conditions require. No claim is priced with the exponent $\beta_H$ before the switch or with the unconditional coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}$ in place of a regime-contingent value.



\textbf{The nested pure-power game: leader scale.} The nested game holds the leader's $(K_L, \phi_L)$ at the monopoly-phase pure-power policy of \texttt{sec-single-firm.} Because $X_P$ equalizes rents against an $L(\cdot)$ evaluated at that fixed scale, the preemption discount inherits the convention, and this block reports how much inside the nested game. The alternative solved here lets the leader choose scale and allocation \emph{for entry at the entry point itself}: the leader's value of entering at $X$ is the upper envelope

\begin{equation*}
L^{\text{re}}(X) = \max_{K, \phi}\, L(X; K, \phi),
\end{equation*}

with the follower best-responding to the chosen $(K, \phi)$, and the trigger solves the fixed point $L^{\text{re}}(X_P) = F\bigl(X_P; K_L^{\text{re}}(X_P), \phi_L^{\text{re}}(X_P)\bigr)$. Everything else is held fixed (the unconditional-$A_{\text{eff}}$ discounting, the single default boundary, the par-debt convention), so the comparison isolates the leader-scale convention alone. Computationally, the envelope gap is evaluated on a 40-point log grid over $(10^{-3} X_L^{\text{mono}},\, X_L^{\text{mono}})$ with the leader's two-dimensional Nelder--Mead optimizer warm-started along the grid (a 6-point deterministic multistart at the first node), the first up-crossing is refined with Brent's method, and the resulting policy is re-checked against the 16-start follower solver. Exactly one up-crossing is found in each case reported.



\textbf{Coupled default boundary.} The single-boundary default formula (\texttt{eq-default-boundary}), which Proposition 2 and the credit exhibits use, is compared with the fully coupled regime-switching system, which the preemption game of Proposition 3 uses: the H-regime equity has the closed Leland form $E_H(X) = A_H(\phi K)^\alpha s^H X - (C_D + \delta K)/r + D_H X^{\beta_H^-}$, whose default-option term forces an additional particular solution $C_2 X^{\beta_H^-}$ in the L-regime equity ODE; value matching and smooth pasting at the boundary then determine $X_D$ jointly with the homogeneous coefficient $A_-$. Because $A_-$ enters both boundary conditions linearly, the combination $\beta_L^- E(X_D) - X_D E'(X_D) = 0$ eliminates it exactly, reducing the coupled system to a single equation,

\begin{equation*}
A_{\text{eff}}\,(\beta_L^- - 1)\,X_D - \beta_L^- N + C_2\,(\beta_L^- - \beta_H^-)\,X_D^{\beta_H^-} = 0, \qquad N = \frac{C_D + \delta K}{r},
\end{equation*}



whose economically relevant root (the continuation of the single-boundary root as $C_2 \to 0$) is computed by Brent's method. A first-order expansion in the small coefficient $C_2$ around the single-boundary root $X_D^0$ gives the closed-form relative bias

\begin{equation*}
\frac{X_D^0 - X_D}{X_D^0} \;\approx\; \eta = \frac{C_2\,(\beta_L^- - \beta_H^-)\,(X_D^0)^{\beta_H^- - 1}}{A_{\text{eff}}\,(\beta_L^- - 1)} > 0,
\end{equation*}

positive because $C_2 < 0$ at calibration values. The expansion therefore gives a closed-form explanation of the direction of the bias, namely that the single-boundary formula overstates default risk, with the sign of $C_2$ evaluated at calibration values rather than signed in general. At baseline the exact relative bias is 3.1\\% and the first-order $\eta$ is 2.9\\%, uniform across leverage levels; the closed-form boundary exceeds the coupled-system boundary by approximately 3\\% throughout, in the conservative direction. The scalar equation presumes that the claim held after the switch is alive at the L-regime boundary, that is $X_D^L \geq X_D^H$. That holds for an installed monopolist and fails for a small firm facing a large rival, which survives before the switch only on the prospect of the switch: for the baseline leader against the baseline follower's capacity the post-switch boundary is the higher of the two. The preemption game therefore solves the boundary from the piecewise forcing, in which the post-switch claim is zero below its own boundary, and reproduces the scalar equation to ten digits where its premise holds.



\textbf{The nested pure-power game: separable reduction of the follower problem.} Proposition 3(i) is the exact counterpart of this reduction, with all capacity in training and $A_H$ in place of $g(\phi)$. In the nested game the follower enters before the switch and chooses $\phi_F$. At a common training fraction $\phi_F = \phi_L = \phi$, the Tullock denominators factor, since $[(1-\phi)K_F]^\alpha + [(1-\phi)K_L]^\alpha = (1-\phi)^\alpha (K_F^\alpha + K_L^\alpha)$ and likewise for the training measure, so the follower's effective revenue coefficient separates exactly as in Proposition 1:

\begin{equation*}
A_{\text{eff},F} = g(\phi) \cdot \frac{K_F^{2\alpha}}{K_F^\alpha + K_L^\alpha},
\end{equation*}



with $g(\phi) = w_L (1-\phi)^\alpha + w_H \phi^\alpha$. The allocation FOC is then exactly the single-firm condition (the role-invariance of Proposition 3(ii)), and the capacity FOC reduces to a single equation with \emph{effective revenue elasticity} $\alpha(2 - s_F)$, where $s_F = K_F^\alpha/(K_F^\alpha + K_L^\alpha)$:

\begin{equation*}
\alpha \beta_H\,\bigl(2 - s_F(K_F)\bigr)\, \Theta_\ell(K_F) = (\beta_H - 1)\, K_F\, \Theta_\ell'(K_F),
\end{equation*}

where $\Theta_\ell(K) = \delta K / r + c[1 - \ell(1 - r_c/r)]K^\gamma$ is the leverage-adjusted total cost. The left-hand bracket $\alpha\beta_H(2 - s_F) - (\beta_H - 1)K\Theta_\ell'/\Theta_\ell$ is strictly decreasing in $K$ ($s_F$ is increasing and $K\Theta_\ell'/\Theta_\ell$ rises from 1 to $\gamma$), so the interior optimum is \emph{unique} whenever $(\beta_H - 1)/(2\alpha\beta_H) < 1$ and $(\beta_H - 1)/(\alpha\beta_H) > 1/\gamma$. The first condition is weaker than (A2)'s upper bound because the follower's small-$K$ elasticity is $2\alpha$ (share gains compound the standalone revenue gain), so the follower's problem remains well-posed in part of the region where the single-firm problem degenerates. The scalar solution agrees with the two-dimensional Nelder-Mead optimizer to a relative tolerance of $10^{-6}$ at baseline (with and without leverage), which the code repository's test suite enforces as an automated check; the elasticity wedge $\alpha(2 - s_F) > \alpha$ is the analytical source of the large follower scale ($K_F \gg K_L$) discussed in \texttt{sec-duopoly} and \texttt{sec-calibration.}

\subsection*{G. A Normalized Scale-Gap Diagnostic}

1. \textbf{Assets-in-place}: the value of existing installed capacity at current demand, incorporating both L-regime inference revenue and H-regime continuation value through $A_{\text{eff}}$.

\begin{equation*}
V_{\text{AIP}} = A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, K_{\text{installed}}) \cdot X - \frac{\delta K_{\text{installed}}}{r}.
\end{equation*}



2. \textbf{Capacity gap value}: the shortfall of the current installed base relative to the optimally sized project,

\begin{equation*}
V_{\text{gap}} = \max\{\text{NPV}(K^*, \phi^*) - V_{\text{AIP}},\; 0\},
\end{equation*}

where $\text{NPV}(K^*, \phi^*)$ is the net (of the full investment cost $I(K^*)$) present value of the optimally sized greenfield project. This is a comparative-statics measure of distance to optimal scale, namely how far the firm's gross installed-asset value falls short of the net value of a full-scale deployment. It is not the NPV of incremental expansion from the installed base (which would credit the firm for capacity already sunk), and it is not a forward-looking option value. Because the benchmark nets out the entire investment cost while assets-in-place are gross of sunk costs, the gap reaches zero before $K_{\text{installed}}$ reaches $K^*$.



The value of the possibility of transitioning from $L$ to $H$ does not appear as a third additive term: it is embedded in \emph{both} quantities through the effective revenue coefficient $A_{\text{eff}}(\phi, \cdot)$, which already weights the H-regime continuation value by the arrival rate $\lambda$ and the training allocation $\phi$. The scale-gap index is then

\begin{equation*}
g(K_{\text{installed}}) = \frac{V_{\text{gap}}}{V_{\text{AIP}} + V_{\text{gap}}} \in [0, 1].
\end{equation*}



\subsection*{H. Credit Spreads and Default Probabilities}

\textbf{Credit spreads.} For debt with coupon flow $C_D$, the credit spread is:

\begin{equation*}
\text{spread} = \frac{C_D}{D(X)} - r,
\end{equation*}

where $D(X)$ is the market value of the debt at its issuance demand $X$ (which differs from the default-free value $C_D/r$ because of default risk), $C_D = r_c \ell I(K)$ under par debt and the coupon at which $D(X) = \ell I(K)$ under fairly priced debt, and the reference rate is the model's discount rate $r$ (the WACC), not a risk-free rate. Under fairly priced debt the spread is the coupon rate on the proceeds less $r$. The debt values below are those of the entry game (Internet Appendix B): the boundary is the one of the coupled regime-switching problem, default can occur after the switch at the H-regime boundary, and recovery follows \texttt{eq-recovery.} Because leverage and the coupon rate are exogenous stress-test parameters (\texttt{sec-model}), the leverage gradients below describe the model's response to an imposed debt burden at a fixed policy, not an optimally chosen capital structure.



\textbf{Default probability.} The probability of default within horizon $T$ is the first-passage probability for GBM hitting the barrier $X_D$:

\begin{equation*}
P(\text{default within } T) = \mathcal{N}(-d_1) + \left(\frac{X_D}{X}\right)^{2\nu/\sigma^2} \mathcal{N}(-d_2),
\end{equation*}

where $\nu = \mu_s - \sigma^2/2$ with $s$ the regime in which the firm enters, $d_1 = [\ln(X/X_D) + \nu T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, $d_2 = [\ln(X/X_D) - \nu T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, and $\mathcal{N}$ is the standard normal CDF. This is the exact barrier hitting probability for GBM, consistent with the Leland-style first-passage default mechanism in the model. For a firm that enters before the switch the drift is $\mu_L$ and the calculation abstracts from the switch itself, since a switch to $H$ before hitting $X_D$ replaces the boundary by the higher-drift H-regime problem, so the reported figures are upper bounds on the pre-switch default probability; for the follower, which enters after the switch, the drift is $\mu_H$. Since $\mu_s$ is the risk-adjusted (certainty-equivalent) drift, the result is a \emph{model-implied risk-adjusted} first-passage probability, computed under the same convention as the spread calculation. It is not a risk-neutral (pricing-measure) probability, because the model discounts at the WACC rather than at a risk-free rate (see the footnote in \texttt{sec-model}). The physical-measure probability, using the unadjusted drift, would be lower.
